In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the divergence in productivity growth between Australia (and New Zealand) has been due to the combined effects of a large contribution from differences in labour input and a large contribution from cross-country structural differences.

there is little evidence of convergence in market sector productivity between Australia and New Zealand, with most of the divergence arising from labour growth and structural factors, and that the industries that add to the divergence are the mining and wholesale industries.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Australia and New Zealand have been growing at a similar rate in the market sector, but the composition of that growth has been different.
the cross-country productivity divergence between New Zealand and Australia has been driven primarily by differences in labour growth.
the divergence in productivity growth between Australia (AUS) and New Zealand (NZ) is driven by differences in labour growth.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the divergence in productivity growth between the two countries is driven by a combination of structural and industry differences, and that these differences are likely to be persistent.
the industry-level contributors are large, and the industry-level decomposition can be used to identify the industries that are most important for productivity convergence.
the decomposition provides an important tool for policy analysis and for identifying the key drivers of aggregate productivity growth.
